entry.title: Rotation Representations
entry.content:
Every robot that carries an IMU has to answer one question many times a second: which way am I facing? There are three common ways to write the answer down: a rotation matrix, three Euler angles, or a unit quaternion. This post builds all three from scratch. It starts in the plane, where complex numbers already know how to rotate, and then follows the same idea into three dimensions until quaternions fall out on their own.

Along the way we will meet the single most useful habit for this topic: reading the same matrix in two ways, as a rotation that moves a vector (active) and as a change of coordinates between two frames (passive). The outline follows Ben-Ari's tutorial [1].

1. Rotations in the plane

1.1 Rotating a vector

Take a vector \(\mathbf{v} = (x, y)\) of length \(r\) that makes an angle \(\varphi\) with the \(x\)-axis, so that \(x = r\cos\varphi\) and \(y = r\sin\varphi\). Rotating it counterclockwise by \(\theta\) keeps the length and adds \(\theta\) to the angle.

With the angle-sum formulas,

\[ \begin{aligned} x' &= r\cos(\varphi + \theta) = r\cos\varphi\cos\theta - r\sin\varphi\sin\theta = x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta, \\ y' &= r\sin(\varphi + \theta) = r\sin\varphi\cos\theta + r\cos\varphi\sin\theta = x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta, \end{aligned} \]

or, as a matrix,

\[ \begin{equation} \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}}_{R(\theta)} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}. \label{eq:R2} \end{equation} \]

1.2 The columns are the rotated axes

There is a faster way to find \(R(\theta)\), and it is the one we will use in 3D. A matrix times the basis vector \(\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)\) gives its first column, and times \(\mathbf{e}_2 = (0, 1)\) gives its second column. So we only need to know where the two axes go:

\[ R\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad R\mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} R\mathbf{e}_1 & R\mathbf{e}_2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

A few properties follow directly and carry over to 3D:

  • The columns are orthonormal, so \(R^\top R = I\) and the inverse is just the transpose: \(R(\theta)^{-1} = R(-\theta) = R(\theta)^\top\).
  • \(\det R = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\): a rotation never mirrors.
  • Rotations add: \(R(\alpha)R(\beta) = R(\alpha + \beta)\). In particular, 2D rotations commute. This will fail in 3D.

1.3 Complex numbers and Euler's formula

Now encode the vector \((x, y)\) as the complex number \(z = x + iy\). (Engineers usually write \(j\) for the imaginary unit; I use \(i\) here because \(j\) will get a different job in Section 4.) The key fact is Euler's formula:

\[ \begin{equation} e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta. \label{eq:euler} \end{equation} \]

It follows from the Taylor series of \(e^x\). Because \(i^2 = -1\), the even powers of \(i\theta\) are real and alternate in sign, and the odd powers are imaginary:

\[ e^{i\theta} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(i\theta)^n}{n!} = \underbrace{\left(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!} - \cdots\right)}_{\cos\theta} + i\underbrace{\left(\theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!} - \cdots\right)}_{\sin\theta}. \]

Writing \(z\) in polar form, \(z = r e^{i\varphi}\), a rotation becomes a single multiplication:

\[ e^{i\theta} z = r\,e^{i(\varphi + \theta)}. \]

The length stays \(r\) and the angle grows by \(\theta\), which is exactly Figure 1. Expanding the product gives back the matrix \(\eqref{eq:R2}\):

\[ (\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)(x + iy) = (x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta) + i\,(x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta). \]

Three ideas from this section drive everything that follows:

  1. A vector is a number built from an imaginary unit: \((x, y) \leftrightarrow x + iy\).
  2. A rotation is multiplication by a number of length one, \(e^{i\theta}\). Composing rotations is multiplying numbers.
  3. The imaginary unit generates the rotation. Multiplying by \(i\) itself rotates by \(90^\circ\), and \(e^{i\theta}\) is “\(i\) applied a fraction \(\theta / (\pi/2)\) of the way”.

2. Rotations and frames

2.1 Axis, angle and the right-hand rule

In 3D, every rotation turns space about some axis, a unit vector \(\mathbf{n}\), by some angle \(\theta\). (This is Euler's rotation theorem.) To say which way is positive we use the right-hand rule: point the thumb of your right hand along \(\mathbf{n}\); your fingers curl in the positive direction. Equivalently, looking from the tip of \(\mathbf{n}\) back toward the origin, a positive rotation is counterclockwise.

The same rule fixes the frames themselves: a frame is right-handed when \(\mathbf{e}_1 \times \mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{e}_3\). It also defines the angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = \dot\theta\,\mathbf{n}\): its direction is the axis, and its length is how fast the body turns. A gyroscope measures exactly this vector, in the coordinates of the sensor's own frame.

A 3D rotation matrix has orthonormal columns and determinant \(+1\): \(R^\top R = I\), \(\det R = 1\). As in 2D, its inverse is its transpose.

2.2 Two ways to read a rotation matrix

The equation \(\mathbf{y} = R\mathbf{x}\) can mean two different things, and mixing them up is the source of most sign and order bugs.

Active reading (a rotation). There is one frame. \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}' = R\mathbf{x}\) are coordinates in that same frame, and \(R\) moves the vector to a new place. This is what Section 1 did.

Passive reading (a frame transformation). There is one point \(p\) and two frames: a world frame \(W\), with axes \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\), and a body frame \(B\) attached to the robot, with axes \(\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \mathbf{b}_3\). The body coordinates \(\mathbf{x}_B\) of the point say how to reach it along the body axes:

\[ p = x_{B,1}\,\mathbf{b}_1 + x_{B,2}\,\mathbf{b}_2 + x_{B,3}\,\mathbf{b}_3. \]

To get world coordinates, write each body axis in world coordinates, \([\mathbf{b}_k]_W\), and collect them as columns:

\[ \begin{equation} \mathbf{x}_W = x_{B,1}[\mathbf{b}_1]_W + x_{B,2}[\mathbf{b}_2]_W + x_{B,3}[\mathbf{b}_3]_W = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} [\mathbf{b}_1]_W & [\mathbf{b}_2]_W & [\mathbf{b}_3]_W \end{bmatrix}}_{R_{WB}} \mathbf{x}_B . \label{eq:passive} \end{equation} \]

So the columns of \(R_{WB}\) are the body axes written in world coordinates. Its rows are the world axes written in body coordinates, because \(R_{BW} = R_{WB}^{-1} = R_{WB}^\top\). Nothing moves here: \(\mathbf{x}_B\) and \(\mathbf{x}_W\) describe the same point, and \(R_{WB}\) only rewrites its coordinates.

How the two readings connect. Apply \(R_{WB}\) actively to the world axes: \(R_{WB}\mathbf{e}_k\) is the \(k\)-th column, which is \([\mathbf{b}_k]_W\). So \(R_{WB}\) is also the rotation that carries the world frame onto the body frame. “The body is rotated by \(R_{WB}\)” and “\(\mathbf{x}_W = R_{WB}\mathbf{x}_B\)” are the same matrix, read two ways.

The subscripts make the passive reading almost mechanical. \(R_{AB}\) takes \(B\)-coordinates to \(A\)-coordinates, and adjacent subscripts cancel:

\[ \mathbf{x}_A = R_{AB}\,\mathbf{x}_B, \qquad R_{AC} = R_{AB}\,R_{BC}, \qquad R_{BA} = R_{AB}^{-1} = R_{AB}^\top . \]

Example. A robot has turned \(90^\circ\) to the left, so \(R_{WB} = R(90^\circ) = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) (in the plane). A point one meter straight ahead of the robot has \(\mathbf{x}_B = (1, 0)\), so \(\mathbf{x}_W = R_{WB}\mathbf{x}_B = (0, 1)\): one meter along the world \(y\)-axis, which is where the robot is now facing.

Why the passive reading is the useful one. On a robot, sensors measure in the body frame and goals live in the world frame. A gyroscope gives \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_B\). An accelerometer at rest measures the reaction to gravity in body coordinates, \(\mathbf{a}_B = R_{WB}^\top (0, 0, g)^\top\), and comparing that with the known world vector is how a filter such as Mahony's corrects its attitude. Every one of these steps is a change of frame, not a motion.

3. Euler angles

3.1 Rotations about one axis

We build the three elementary rotations the way we built \(R(\theta)\) in Section 1.2: find where each axis goes, and use the results as columns. In each case, look down the rotation axis from its tip, so that the rotation is counterclockwise and the other two axes behave like the 2D plane.

About \(x\) by the roll angle \(\varphi\). The \(x\)-axis does not move. In the \((y, z)\) plane, \(y\) plays the role of the 2D \(x\)-axis and \(z\) the role of the 2D \(y\)-axis:

\[ R_x\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},\quad R_x\mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \cos\varphi \\ \sin\varphi \end{bmatrix},\quad R_x\mathbf{e}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\sin\varphi \\ \cos\varphi \end{bmatrix}, \]

so

\[ R_x(\varphi) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi \\ 0 & \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi \end{bmatrix}. \]

About \(z\) by the yaw angle \(\psi\). This is the 2D rotation with \(z\) left alone:

\[ R_z\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\psi \\ \sin\psi \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},\quad R_z\mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin\psi \\ \cos\psi \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},\quad R_z\mathbf{e}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

so

\[ R_z(\psi) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\psi & -\sin\psi & 0 \\ \sin\psi & \cos\psi & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

About \(y\) by the pitch angle \(\theta\). Here the cyclic order matters. After \(y\) comes \(z\), then \(x\), so in the \((z, x)\) plane it is \(z\) that plays the role of the 2D \(x\)-axis. A positive rotation turns \(z\) toward \(x\), and \(x\) toward \(-z\):

\[ R_y\mathbf{e}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta \\ 0 \\ \cos\theta \end{bmatrix},\quad R_y\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta \\ 0 \\ -\sin\theta \end{bmatrix},\quad R_y\mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \]

so

\[ R_y(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}. \]

The minus sign sits below the diagonal in \(R_y\) but above it in \(R_x\) and \(R_z\). That is not a typo: listing the rows in the order \(x, y, z\) writes the \((z, x)\) plane backwards. (A side effect: with \(z\) pointing up, a positive pitch tips the nose, the \(x\)-axis, down.)

3.2 The order matters

Unlike in the plane, rotations about different axes do not commute. Follow \(\mathbf{e}_1\) through two quarter turns:

\[ R_z(90^\circ)\,R_x(90^\circ)\,\mathbf{e}_1 = R_z(90^\circ)\,\mathbf{e}_1 = \mathbf{e}_2, \qquad R_x(90^\circ)\,R_z(90^\circ)\,\mathbf{e}_1 = R_x(90^\circ)\,\mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{e}_3 . \]

Same two rotations, different results. So “three Euler angles” means nothing until we also fix the order of the axes. There are 12 possible orders (any sequence of three axes with no axis twice in a row).

3.3 Yaw, pitch, roll: \(R_{WB} = R_z(\psi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_x(\varphi)\)

The usual choice in robotics and aerospace, and the one in my IMU code, is the Z-Y-X order: yaw \(\psi\) about \(z\), pitch \(\theta\) about \(y\), roll \(\varphi\) about \(x\),

\[ \begin{equation} R_{WB} = R_z(\psi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_x(\varphi). \label{eq:zyx} \end{equation} \]

Note the order of the factors: \(z\) on the left, \(x\) on the right. Writing \(R_x R_y R_z\) gives a different (and much less common) convention. The two readings from Section 2.2 explain the order.

Active reading: rotations about the fixed world axes. Applied to a vector, \(R_z(\psi)\big(R_y(\theta)(R_x(\varphi)\, \mathbf{v})\big)\) acts right to left: first roll about the world \(x\)-axis, then pitch about the world \(y\)-axis, then yaw about the world \(z\)-axis. The axes stay fixed, and the order is \(x\), then \(y\), then \(z\).

Passive reading: a chain of frames. Insert two intermediate frames, \(1\) and \(2\), and read \(\eqref{eq:zyx}\) as the chain rule of Section 2.2:

\[ \mathbf{x}_W = \underbrace{R_z(\psi)}_{R_{W1}}\ \underbrace{R_y(\theta)}_{R_{12}}\ \underbrace{R_x(\varphi)}_{R_{2B}}\ \mathbf{x}_B . \]

Each factor is an elementary rotation about an axis of the frame before it. Frame 1 is the world frame yawed by \(\psi\) about \(z_W\). Frame 2 is frame 1 pitched by \(\theta\) about its own \(y_1\)-axis. The body frame is frame 2 rolled by \(\varphi\) about its own \(x_2\)-axis. The axes move with the body, and the order is \(z\), then \(y\), then \(x\). This is how we naturally describe a robot or a plane: heading first, then tilt, then bank.

Both readings describe the same matrix: rotating about the moving axes in the order \(z, y, x\) equals rotating about the fixed axes in the order \(x, y, z\). Multiplying out, with \(c_\varphi = \cos\varphi\), \(s_\varphi = \sin\varphi\) and so on:

\[ \begin{equation} R_{WB} = \begin{bmatrix} c_\psi c_\theta & c_\psi s_\theta s_\varphi - s_\psi c_\varphi & c_\psi s_\theta c_\varphi + s_\psi s_\varphi \\ s_\psi c_\theta & s_\psi s_\theta s_\varphi + c_\psi c_\varphi & s_\psi s_\theta c_\varphi - c_\psi s_\varphi \\ -s_\theta & c_\theta s_\varphi & c_\theta c_\varphi \end{bmatrix}. \label{eq:Rzyx} \end{equation} \]

The angles can be read back from the entries \(r_{ij}\). The bottom-left entry gives the pitch, and the ratios in the last row and the first column give roll and yaw:

\[ \theta = -\arcsin r_{31}, \qquad \varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(r_{32},\, r_{33}), \qquad \psi = \operatorname{atan2}(r_{21},\, r_{11}). \]

3.4 Gimbal lock

The read-back fails when \(\cos\theta = 0\), i.e. pitch \(\theta = \pm 90^\circ\). Then \(r_{11} = r_{21} = r_{32} = r_{33} = 0\) and both \(\operatorname{atan2}\) calls become \(\operatorname{atan2}(0, 0)\). Substituting \(\theta = 90^\circ\) into \(\eqref{eq:Rzyx}\) shows why:

\[ R_{WB}\big|_{\theta = 90^\circ} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \sin(\varphi - \psi) & \cos(\varphi - \psi) \\ 0 & \cos(\varphi - \psi) & -\sin(\varphi - \psi) \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The matrix depends only on \(\varphi - \psi\). Every pair \((\varphi, \psi)\) with the same difference gives the same orientation, so one degree of freedom has disappeared. (At \(\theta = -90^\circ\) it is \(\varphi + \psi\) instead.)

Geometrically, pitching by \(90^\circ\) swings the roll axis onto the yaw axis, so the two rotations do the same thing. Near this pitch, small changes in orientation cause huge jumps in \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\). Nothing is wrong with the orientation itself; the problem is the parametrization. In fact, every description of 3D rotations by three numbers has singular points like this one. Using four numbers avoids it, which brings us to quaternions.

4. Quaternions

4.1 From the plane to space: what must \(i, j, k\) be?

Let us redo Section 1.3 in three dimensions without assuming anything about quaternions. In the plane, one imaginary unit was enough. In space, give each axis its own unit and write a vector as

\[ \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z) \ \longleftrightarrow\ v = x\,i + y\,j + z\,k . \]

We want to multiply such numbers, and we want the rules for \(i, j, k\) to be forced by a few reasonable requirements.

(R1) Each unit is an imaginary unit: \(i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = -1\), just like \(i\) in the plane.

(R2) Squaring a vector gives its length. For complex numbers, \(z\bar z = |z|^2\). Here we ask for \(v^2 = -|\mathbf{v}|^2\), so every unit vector is a square root of \(-1\): no axis is special. Expanding, while keeping the order of factors because we have not assumed commutativity,

\[ v^2 = -(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) + xy\,(ij + ji) + yz\,(jk + kj) + zx\,(ki + ik). \]

For this to equal \(-(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)\) for every vector, the units must anticommute:

\[ ji = -ij, \qquad kj = -jk, \qquad ik = -ki . \]

(R3) What is \(ij\)? It cannot be a real number, because \((ij)^2 = ijij = -iijj = -(-1)(-1) = -1\), and no real number squares to \(-1\). Can it be a combination \(a + b\,i + c\,j\) of what we already have? Multiply \(ij = a + bi + cj\) on the left by \(i\). The left side becomes \(i^2 j = -j\), and the right side becomes

\[ ai - b + c\,(ij) = ai - b + c\,(a + bi + cj) = (ca - b) + (a + cb)\,i + c^2\,j . \]

Matching the \(j\) parts needs \(c^2 = -1\), which is impossible for a real \(c\). So \(ij\) is genuinely new. We call it \(k\): \(k = ij\). This is why the 3D version of a complex number needs four components, \(1, i, j, k\), not three.

The remaining products now follow from \(k = ij\) and anticommutation:

\[ \begin{aligned} jk &= j\,(ij) = (ji)\,j = -(ij)\,j = -i\,(jj) = i, \\ ki &= (ij)\,i = i\,(ji) = -i\,(ij) = -(ii)\,j = j, \\ k^2 &= (ij)(ij) = i\,(ji)\,j = -i\,(ij)\,j = -(ii)(jj) = -1 . \end{aligned} \]

Altogether this is Hamilton's multiplication table:

\[ i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1, \qquad ij = k,\ \ jk = i,\ \ ki = j, \qquad ji = -k,\ \ kj = -i,\ \ ik = -j . \]

A quaternion is a number \(q = w + x\,i + y\,j + z\,k\). We write it as a scalar part plus a vector part, \(q = (s, \mathbf{u})\) with \(s = w\) and \(\mathbf{u} = (x, y, z)\). A quaternion with \(s = 0\) is a pure quaternion, which is how vectors live inside the quaternions.

4.2 Multiplication with dot and cross products

Compare the table with the basis vectors \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\). The square \(i^2 = -1\) looks like \(-\mathbf{e}_1\cdot\mathbf{e}_1\), and \(ij = k = -ji\) looks like \(\mathbf{e}_1 \times \mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{e}_3 = -\mathbf{e}_2 \times \mathbf{e}_1\). In general, the product of two units is minus their dot product plus their cross product. By linearity, the same holds for any two pure quaternions:

\[ \begin{equation} \mathbf{u}\,\mathbf{v} = -\,\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} . \label{eq:pure} \end{equation} \]

Adding the scalar parts, the product of two general quaternions is

\[ \begin{equation} (s, \mathbf{u})\,(t, \mathbf{v}) = \big(st - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v},\ \ s\,\mathbf{v} + t\,\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\big). \label{eq:product} \end{equation} \]

This is much easier to remember than the sixteen-term expansion, and it shows at a glance why quaternion multiplication does not commute: the cross product changes sign when the factors swap. (Vince [2] develops all of quaternion algebra in this vector form.) In components it matches the usual formula:

\[ \begin{aligned} (q\,p)_w &= q_w p_w - q_x p_x - q_y p_y - q_z p_z, \\ (q\,p)_x &= q_w p_x + q_x p_w + q_y p_z - q_z p_y, \\ (q\,p)_y &= q_w p_y + q_y p_w + q_z p_x - q_x p_z, \\ (q\,p)_z &= q_w p_z + q_z p_w + q_x p_y - q_y p_x . \end{aligned} \]

Some further facts we will need, each a one-line check with \(\eqref{eq:product}\):

  • The conjugate is \(q^* = (s, -\mathbf{u})\), and \((qp)^* = p^*q^*\).
  • The norm satisfies \(qq^* = q^*q = s^2 + |\mathbf{u}|^2 = |q|^2\) and \(|qp| = |q|\,|p|\).
  • The inverse is \(q^{-1} = q^*/|q|^2\). For a unit quaternion (\(|q| = 1\)), \(q^{-1} = q^*\).
  • For a unit vector \(\mathbf{n}\), \(\eqref{eq:pure}\) gives \(\mathbf{n}^2 = -1\). The Taylor-series argument of Section 1.3 then repeats word for word: \(e^{\mathbf{n}\alpha} = \cos\alpha + \mathbf{n}\sin\alpha\). Every unit vector is an “\(i\)” with its own Euler formula.

4.3 Rotating a vector, and the half angle

First attempt. Copy the plane: multiply \(\mathbf{v}\) by \(q = e^{\mathbf{n}\alpha} = \cos\alpha + \mathbf{n}\sin\alpha\). By \(\eqref{eq:product}\),

\[ q\,\mathbf{v} = \big(-\sin\alpha\ \mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{v},\ \ \cos\alpha\,\mathbf{v} + \sin\alpha\,\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{v}\big). \]

If \(\mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{n}\), the scalar part vanishes and the vector part, \(\cos\alpha\,\mathbf{v} + \sin\alpha\,\mathbf{n}\times \mathbf{v}\), is exactly \(\mathbf{v}\) rotated by \(\alpha\) about \(\mathbf{n}\), because \(\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{v}\) is \(\mathbf{v}\) turned \(90^\circ\) about \(\mathbf{n}\). That is the plane all over again. But if \(\mathbf{v}\) has a component along \(\mathbf{n}\), the result has a scalar part and is no longer a vector.

The fix: the sandwich \(q\,\mathbf{v}\,q^*\). Split \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}_\parallel + \mathbf{v}_\perp\) into the parts along and across \(\mathbf{n}\), and use \(\eqref{eq:pure}\) to see how each part commutes with \(\mathbf{n}\):

\[ \mathbf{n}\,\mathbf{v}_\parallel = -\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{v}_\parallel = \mathbf{v}_\parallel\,\mathbf{n}, \qquad \mathbf{n}\,\mathbf{v}_\perp = \mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{v}_\perp = -\,\mathbf{v}_\perp\times\mathbf{n} = -\,\mathbf{v}_\perp\,\mathbf{n} . \]

So \(\mathbf{v}_\parallel\) commutes with \(q = \cos\alpha + \mathbf{n}\sin\alpha\), while \(\mathbf{v}_\perp\) flips the sign of the \(\mathbf{n}\) term as it passes through: \(\mathbf{v}_\perp\,q^* = q\,\mathbf{v}_\perp\). Therefore

\[ \begin{aligned} q\,\mathbf{v}_\parallel\,q^* &= \mathbf{v}_\parallel\,q\,q^* = \mathbf{v}_\parallel, \\ q\,\mathbf{v}_\perp\,q^* &= q\,q\,\mathbf{v}_\perp = e^{2\alpha\mathbf{n}}\,\mathbf{v}_\perp = \cos 2\alpha\ \mathbf{v}_\perp + \sin 2\alpha\ \mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{v}_\perp . \end{aligned} \]

The part along the axis is untouched, and the part across it turns by \(2\alpha\). That is a rotation by \(2\alpha\) about \(\mathbf{n}\), and the result is a pure quaternion again. To rotate by \(\theta\), take \(\alpha = \theta/2\):

\[ \begin{equation} \boxed{\ q = e^{\mathbf{n}\theta/2} = \Big(\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\ \ \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,\mathbf{n}\Big), \qquad \mathbf{v}' = q\,\mathbf{v}\,q^* = \mathbf{v}_\parallel + \cos\theta\ \mathbf{v}_\perp + \sin\theta\ \mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{v}\ } \label{eq:sandwich} \end{equation} \]

(Note \(\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{v}_\perp\). The right-hand side is Rodrigues' rotation formula.) The half angle appears because \(q\) acts twice, once from each side. Two consequences:

  • \(q\) and \(-q\) give the same rotation, since the two minus signs cancel in \(q\,\mathbf{v}\,q^*\). Every rotation has exactly two unit quaternions.
  • Every unit quaternion is a rotation: any \(q\) with \(|q| = 1\) can be written as \((\cos\frac\theta2, \sin\frac\theta2\,\mathbf{n})\).

Back to the plane. Take \(\mathbf{n} = k\) and a vector in the \(xy\)-plane, \(\mathbf{v} = x\,i + y\,j \perp k\). Then \(q\,\mathbf{v}\,q^* = q^2\,\mathbf{v} = (\cos\theta + k\sin\theta)(x\,i + y\,j)\), and with \(ki = j\) and \(kj = -i\),

\[ (\cos\theta + k\sin\theta)(x\,i + y\,j) = (x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta)\,i + (x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta)\,j , \]

which is the 2D rotation \(\eqref{eq:R2}\). The quaternion \(k\) plays exactly the role that \(i\) played in the complex plane.

Example. Rotate \(\mathbf{e}_1 = i\) by \(90^\circ\) about \(z\). Here \(q = \cos 45^\circ + k\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}(1 + k)\). Since \(i \perp k\), \(q\,i\,q^* = q^2\,i = k\,i = j\), so the result is \(\mathbf{e}_2\), as it should be.

4.4 Composition and frames

Quaternions compose like matrices. Rotating by \(q_1\) and then by \(q_2\):

\[ q_2\,(q_1\,\mathbf{v}\,q_1^*)\,q_2^* = (q_2 q_1)\,\mathbf{v}\,(q_2 q_1)^* , \]

so the combined rotation is \(q_2 q_1\), in the same order as \(R_2 R_1\). Everything from the passive reading carries over. Let \(q_{WB}\) be the quaternion of \(R_{WB}\). Then

\[ \mathbf{x}_W = q_{WB}\,\mathbf{x}_B\,q_{WB}^*, \qquad q_{WC} = q_{WB}\,q_{BC}, \qquad q_{BW} = q_{WB}^* . \]

From Euler angles. Each elementary rotation is a rotation about a basis axis, so by \(\eqref{eq:sandwich}\), \(q_x(\varphi) = \cos\frac\varphi2 + i\sin\frac\varphi2\), \(q_y(\theta) = \cos\frac\theta2 + j\sin\frac\theta2\), and \(q_z(\psi) = \cos\frac\psi2 + k\sin\frac\psi2\). Multiplying them in the same order as \(\eqref{eq:zyx}\), \(q_{WB} = q_z(\psi)\,q_y(\theta)\,q_x(\varphi)\), and writing \(c_\varphi = \cos\frac\varphi2\), \(s_\varphi = \sin\frac\varphi2\) (half angles this time):

\[ \begin{aligned} w &= c_\varphi c_\theta c_\psi + s_\varphi s_\theta s_\psi, & x &= s_\varphi c_\theta c_\psi - c_\varphi s_\theta s_\psi, \\ y &= c_\varphi s_\theta c_\psi + s_\varphi c_\theta s_\psi, & z &= c_\varphi c_\theta s_\psi - s_\varphi s_\theta c_\psi . \end{aligned} \]

Integrating a gyroscope. The passive reading also tells us how to update the orientation from gyroscope readings. Over a short time \(\Delta t\), the body turns by the small angle \(|\boldsymbol\omega|\Delta t\) about \(\boldsymbol\omega_B\), expressed in its own frame. That small rotation is \(q_{BB'} \approx 1 + \tfrac12\boldsymbol\omega_B\Delta t\), and the chain rule puts it on the right: \(q_{WB'} = q_{WB}\,q_{BB'}\). Letting \(\Delta t \to 0\) gives the quaternion kinematics used in attitude filters [3]:

\[ \dot q_{WB} = \tfrac12\, q_{WB} \otimes (0,\ \boldsymbol\omega_B). \]

4.5 From a quaternion to a rotation matrix

Expanding the sandwich with \(\eqref{eq:product}\) gives a formula that needs no trigonometry. For a unit \(q = (s, \mathbf{u})\), first \(q\,\mathbf{v} = (-\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v},\ s\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\). Multiplying on the right by \(q^* = (s, -\mathbf{u})\), the scalar part cancels and the vector part is

\[ (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{u} + s^2\,\mathbf{v} + 2s\,\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} - (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\times\mathbf{u} . \]

With the identity \((\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\times\mathbf{u} = |\mathbf{u}|^2\mathbf{v} - (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{u}\),

\[ \begin{equation} q\,\mathbf{v}\,q^* = (s^2 - |\mathbf{u}|^2)\,\mathbf{v} + 2\,(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{u} + 2s\,\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} . \label{eq:qvq} \end{equation} \]

Each term is linear in \(\mathbf{v}\), so this is a matrix: \(R = (s^2 - |\mathbf{u}|^2)\,I + 2\,\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top + 2s\,[\mathbf{u}]_\times\), where \([\mathbf{u}]_\times\) is the matrix of \(\mathbf{v} \mapsto \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\). With \(q = (w, x, y, z)\) and \(w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\):

\[ \begin{equation} R(q) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2(y^2 + z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \\ 2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \\ 2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2) \end{bmatrix}. \label{eq:Rq} \end{equation} \]

Going back is just as direct. The trace is \(\operatorname{tr}R = 3 - 4(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) = 4w^2 - 1\), and the off-diagonal differences isolate the vector part:

\[ w = \tfrac12\sqrt{1 + \operatorname{tr}R}, \qquad x = \frac{r_{32} - r_{23}}{4w}, \qquad y = \frac{r_{13} - r_{31}}{4w}, \qquad z = \frac{r_{21} - r_{12}}{4w} . \]

This works as long as \(w\) is not close to zero. For rotations near \(180^\circ\), robust code starts from the largest diagonal entry instead.

4.6 From a quaternion to Euler angles

Now match \(\eqref{eq:Rq}\) against \(\eqref{eq:Rzyx}\) and reuse the read-back formulas from Section 3.3. With \(r_{31} = 2(xz - wy)\), \(r_{32} = 2(yz + wx)\), and so on:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{roll: }\ \varphi &= \operatorname{atan2}\big(2(wx + yz),\ 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2)\big), \\ \text{pitch: }\ \theta &= \arcsin\big(2(wy - xz)\big), \\ \text{yaw: }\ \psi &= \operatorname{atan2}\big(2(wz + xy),\ 1 - 2(y^2 + z^2)\big). \end{aligned} \]

In floating point, clamp the argument of \(\arcsin\) to \([-1, 1]\). Gimbal lock still appears here, as \(2(wy - xz) = \pm 1\), but only in the angles. The quaternion itself is perfectly well behaved there, which is why filters store a quaternion and convert to Euler angles only for display.

5. Summary

Representation Numbers Composition Singularities Good for
Rotation matrix \(R\) 9 (with 6 constraints) \(R_2 R_1\) none transforming many vectors
Euler angles \((\psi, \theta, \varphi)\) 3 through matrices gimbal lock at \(\theta = \pm 90^\circ\) reading and setting by humans
Unit quaternion \(q\) 4 (with 1 constraint) \(q_2 q_1\) none (\(q\) and \(-q\) are the same) integration, filtering, storage

The thread through all of it:

  • In the plane, \(e^{i\theta}\) rotates by multiplication. In space, \(e^{\mathbf{n}\theta/2}\) rotates by the sandwich \(q\,\mathbf{v}\,q^*\).
  • The columns of a rotation matrix are the rotated axes. The columns of \(R_{WB}\) are the body axes in world coordinates.
  • Read \(R_{WB}\) and \(q_{WB}\) passively, and let the subscripts cancel: \(R_{AC} = R_{AB}R_{BC}\), \(q_{AC} = q_{AB}\,q_{BC}\).

References

[1] Moti Ben-Ari. “A Tutorial on Euler Angles and Quaternions.” Weizmann Institute of Science, version 2.0.2, 2014–2017.

[2] John Vince. Quaternions for Computer Graphics. Springer, 2011.

[3] Joan Solà. “Quaternion kinematics for the error-state Kalman filter.” arXiv:1711.02508, 2017.

entry.title: The Sturm–Liouville Problem
entry.content:
Notes on Chapter 11.4 of my MATH 285 course (see also Boyce and DiPrima [1]). This chapter is quite interesting: a second-order ODE turns out to behave exactly like a real symmetric matrix.

The plan is to first recall two facts from linear algebra, then show that the Sturm–Liouville operator is the infinite-dimensional analogue of a symmetric matrix, and finally see why this matters for solving PDEs.

I. Prerequisite: the spectral theorem

For a real symmetric matrix \(A\) (\(A^ op = A\)) of size \(n imes n\):

  1. All eigenvalues \(\lambda\) of \(A\) are real.
  2. Eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j\) for different eigenvalues \(\lambda_i eq \lambda_j\) are orthogonal: \(\mathbf{v}_i \perp \mathbf{v}_j\).
  3. The eigenvectors of \(A\) span all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), so \(A\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

We prove the first two. The third needs a little more work (usually an induction on \(n\)), and we take it as known.

Proof of 1. Let \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{v} eq \mathbf{0}\), where \(\lambda\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) may be complex. Since \(A\) is real, conjugating gives \(A ar{\mathbf{v}} = ar\lambda\, ar{\mathbf{v}}\). Transposing the original equation and using \(A^ op = A\) gives \(\mathbf{v}^ op A = \lambda\,\mathbf{v}^ op\). Now compute \(\mathbf{v}^ op A ar{\mathbf{v}}\) in two ways:

\[ \mathbf{v}^ op A\, ar{\mathbf{v}} = (\mathbf{v}^ op A)\, ar{\mathbf{v}} = \lambda\,\mathbf{v}^ op ar{\mathbf{v}}, \qquad \mathbf{v}^ op A\, ar{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}^ op (A ar{\mathbf{v}}) = ar\lambda\,\mathbf{v}^ op ar{\mathbf{v}} . \]

Since \(\mathbf{v}^ op ar{\mathbf{v}} = \sum_k |v_k|^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 > 0\), we get \(\lambda = ar\lambda\): \(\lambda\) is real.

Proof of 2. Let \(A\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1\) and \(A\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2\) with \(\lambda_1 eq \lambda_2\). Again compute one number in two ways:

\[ \mathbf{v}_1^ op A\,\mathbf{v}_2 = (A\mathbf{v}_1)^ op\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_1\,\mathbf{v}_1^ op\mathbf{v}_2, \qquad \mathbf{v}_1^ op A\,\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_1^ op (A\mathbf{v}_2) = \lambda_2\,\mathbf{v}_1^ op\mathbf{v}_2 . \]

Subtracting, \((\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)\,\mathbf{v}_1^ op\mathbf{v}_2 = 0\). Since \(\lambda_1 eq \lambda_2\), \(\mathbf{v}_1^ op\mathbf{v}_2 = 0\).

Both proofs use only one thing about \(A\): that it can be moved from one side of a dot product to the other, \((A\mathbf{u})^ op\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^ op(A\mathbf{v})\). That is the property we will look for in differential operators.

II. Prerequisite: the inner product of functions

For complex-valued functions on \([a, b]\), define

\[ \langle u, v angle = \int_a^b u^*(t)\,v(t)\,dt , \]

where \(^*\) is complex conjugation. For real functions, \(u^* = u\) and this is just \(\int_a^b u(t)v(t)\,dt\), the continuous version of \(\mathbf{u}^ op\mathbf{v} = \sum_k u_k v_k\). Swapping the arguments conjugates the result:

\[ \overline{\langle v, u angle} = \overline{\int_a^b v^*(t)\,u(t)\,dt} = \int_a^b v(t)\,u^*(t)\,dt = \langle u, v angle . \]

In the real case, \(\langle u, v angle = \langle v, u angle\), just like \(\mathbf{u}^ op\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}^ op\mathbf{u}\). We will also need a weighted inner product, with a weight function \(p(t) > 0\):

\[ \langle u, v angle_p = \int_a^b u^*(t)\,v(t)\,p(t)\,dt . \]

III. Self-adjoint operators

A linear operator \(\mathcal{L}\) is self-adjoint (mathematics) or Hermitian (quantum physics) if

\[ \langle \mathcal{L}u, v angle = \langle u, \mathcal{L}v angle \]

for all \(u, v\) in its domain. For a differential operator, the domain includes the boundary conditions, and as we will see, the boundary conditions are exactly what make this identity hold. For a real matrix, \(\langle A\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} angle = \mathbf{u}^ op A^ op\mathbf{v}\) and \(\langle \mathbf{u}, A\mathbf{v} angle = \mathbf{u}^ op A\mathbf{v}\), so self-adjoint means \(A^ op = A\): a symmetric matrix.

These prerequisites are enough. Now let us set up the Sturm–Liouville problem.

IV. The regular Sturm–Liouville problem

Let \(r(t)\), \(r'(t)\), \(p(t)\) and \(q(t)\) be real functions, continuous on \([a, b]\), with \(r(t) > 0\) and \(p(t) > 0\) on \([a, b]\). We look for numbers \(\lambda\) and nonzero functions \(y\) that solve

\[ egin{equation} rac{d}{dt} ig[r(t)\,y'(t) ig] + ig(q(t) + \lambda\,p(t) ig)\,y(t) = 0 \label{eq:sl} \end{equation} \]

subject to the separated boundary conditions

\[ egin{equation} A_1\,y(a) + B_1\,y'(a) = 0, \qquad A_2\,y(b) + B_2\,y'(b) = 0, \label{eq:bc} \end{equation} \]

where \(A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2\) are real constants with \((A_1, B_1) eq (0, 0)\) and \((A_2, B_2) eq (0, 0)\). Each condition involves only one endpoint. This is a regular Sturm–Liouville problem.

Moving the \(\lambda\) term to the right-hand side,

\[ - rac{d}{dt} ig[r(t)\,y'(t) ig] - q(t)\,y(t) = \lambda\,p(t)\,y(t) . \]

Define the operator

\[ \mathcal{L} = - rac{d}{dt}\left(r(t)\, rac{d}{dt} ight) - q(t) . \]

Then the problem reads

\[ \mathcal{L}\,y = \lambda\,p\,y . \]

This is an eigenvalue problem, the analogue of \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\). We will show that \(\mathcal{L}\) is self-adjoint, and then every property of the spectral theorem carries over.

V. Two properties of the operator

Linearity. For complex-valued functions \(x_1, x_2\) and complex constants \(\alpha, eta\),

\[ egin{aligned} \mathcal{L}\{\alpha x_1 + eta x_2\} &= - rac{d}{dt}\Big[r\,(\alpha x_1' + eta x_2')\Big] - q\,(\alpha x_1 + eta x_2) \ &= \alpha\Big(- rac{d}{dt} ig[r\,x_1' ig] - q\,x_1\Big) + eta\Big(- rac{d}{dt} ig[r\,x_2' ig] - q\,x_2\Big) = \alpha\,\mathcal{L}x_1 + eta\,\mathcal{L}x_2 . \end{aligned} \]

Conjugation. Because \(r\) and \(q\) are real, \(\mathcal{L}\) commutes with complex conjugation: \((\mathcal{L}x)^* = \mathcal{L}\{x^*\}\). Indeed, write \(x = \alpha + i eta\) with \(\alpha, eta\) real functions. Then \(\mathcal{L}\alpha\) and \(\mathcal{L} eta\) are real, and by linearity

\[ (\mathcal{L}x)^* = (\mathcal{L}\alpha + i\,\mathcal{L} eta)^* = \mathcal{L}\alpha - i\,\mathcal{L} eta = \mathcal{L}\{\alpha - i eta\} = \mathcal{L}\{x^*\} . \]

VI. The operator is self-adjoint

We want \(\langle \mathcal{L}u, v angle = \langle u, \mathcal{L}v angle\) for any two functions \(u, v\) that satisfy the boundary conditions \(\eqref{eq:bc}\). Using the conjugation property and integrating by parts once,

\[ egin{aligned} \langle \mathcal{L}u, v angle &= \int_a^b (\mathcal{L}u)^*\,v\,dt = \int_a^b \mathcal{L}\{u^*\}\,v\,dt = \int_a^b \Big(- rac{d}{dt} ig[r\,u^{*\prime} ig] - q\,u^*\Big)\,v\,dt \ &= -\Big[\,r\,u^{*\prime}\,v\,\Big]_a^b + \int_a^b r\,u^{*\prime}\,v'\,dt - \int_a^b q\,u^*\,v\,dt . \end{aligned} \]

In the same way,

\[ \langle u, \mathcal{L}v angle = \int_a^b u^*\,\mathcal{L}v\,dt = -\Big[\,r\,u^*\,v'\,\Big]_a^b + \int_a^b r\,u^{*\prime}\,v'\,dt - \int_a^b q\,u^*\,v\,dt . \]

The two integrals are identical, so only the boundary terms survive in the difference:

\[ egin{equation} \langle \mathcal{L}u, v angle - \langle u, \mathcal{L}v angle = \Big[\,r(t)\, ig(u^*(t)\,v'(t) - u^{*\prime}(t)\,v(t) ig)\Big]_a^b . \label{eq:boundary} \end{equation} \]

The boundary conditions kill the boundary term

Both \(u\) and \(v\) satisfy the condition at \(t = a\). Since \(A_1\) and \(B_1\) are real, conjugating the condition for \(u\) shows that \(u^*\) satisfies it too (using \((u^*)' = (u')^*\)):

\[ A_1\,u^*(a) + B_1\,u^{*\prime}(a) = 0, \qquad A_1\,v(a) + B_1\,v'(a) = 0 . \]

In matrix form,

\[ egin{bmatrix} u^*(a) & u^{*\prime}(a) \ v(a) & v'(a) \end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix} A_1 \ B_1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0} . \]

Since \((A_1, B_1) eq (0, 0)\), this homogeneous system has a nonzero solution, so its determinant must vanish:

\[ u^*(a)\,v'(a) - u^{*\prime}(a)\,v(a) = 0 . \]

The same argument at \(t = b\) gives \(u^*(b)\,v'(b) - u^{*\prime}(b)\,v(b) = 0\). Both ends of \(\eqref{eq:boundary}\) are zero, so

\[ \langle \mathcal{L}u, v angle = \langle u, \mathcal{L}v angle : \]

\(\mathcal{L}\) is self-adjoint. Real-valued functions are a special case of complex-valued ones, so this holds in the real case too. Notice that the proof never used \(r > 0\) or \(p > 0\). Self-adjointness comes from the form of the operator together with the boundary conditions; the positivity of \(r\) and \(p\) matters later.

VII. The spectral theorem for Sturm–Liouville problems

We now get the analogue of the spectral theorem:

  1. All eigenvalues are real.
  2. Eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues are orthogonal with respect to the weight \(p\): \(\langle y_i, y_j angle_p = 0\).
  3. The eigenfunctions form a complete orthogonal basis. The eigenvalues form an infinite increasing sequence \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \cdots o \infty\), and any reasonable function on \([a, b]\) (for example, any square-integrable one) can be expanded in the eigenfunctions, in the sense of the weighted inner product.

The first two follow in a few lines, exactly as for matrices. The third is a deeper theorem [1, 2], which we take as known.

Proof of property 1: the eigenvalues are real

Let \(\mathcal{L}u = \lambda\,p\,u\) with \(u eq 0\). Self-adjointness gives \(\langle u, \mathcal{L}u angle = \langle \mathcal{L}u, u angle\), so

\[ \langle u, \lambda\,p\,u angle = \langle \lambda\,p\,u, u angle \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int_a^b u^*\,\lambda\,p\,u\,dt = \int_a^b (\lambda\,p\,u)^*\,u\,dt . \]

Since \(p\) is real, \(p^* = p\), and this becomes

\[ \lambda \int_a^b p(t)\,|u(t)|^2\,dt = \lambda^* \int_a^b p(t)\,|u(t)|^2\,dt . \]

Because \(p > 0\) and \(u eq 0\), the integral is positive, so \(\lambda = \lambda^*\): \(\lambda\) is real. This is where \(p > 0\) is needed: it makes \(\langle u, u angle_p\) a genuine (positive) squared length.

Proof of property 2: orthogonality

Let \(\mathcal{L}u_1 = \lambda_1\,p\,u_1\) and \(\mathcal{L}u_2 = \lambda_2\,p\,u_2\) with \(\lambda_1 eq \lambda_2\). Self-adjointness gives \(\langle u_1, \mathcal{L}u_2 angle = \langle \mathcal{L}u_1, u_2 angle\), so

\[ \int_a^b u_1^*\,\lambda_2\,p\,u_2\,dt = \int_a^b (\lambda_1\,p\,u_1)^*\,u_2\,dt . \]

Since \(\lambda_1\) is real (property 1) and \(p\) is real,

\[ (\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) \int_a^b u_1^*(t)\,u_2(t)\,p(t)\,dt = 0 . \]

Since \(\lambda_1 eq \lambda_2\),

\[ \langle u_1, u_2 angle_p = \int_a^b u_1^*(t)\,u_2(t)\,p(t)\,dt = 0 . \]

The eigenfunctions are orthogonal, but with respect to the weight \(p\), not the plain inner product. The weight is the coefficient of \(\lambda\) in \(\eqref{eq:sl}\).

VIII. More on Sturm–Liouville problems

1. Why \(r(t) > 0\)?

  • \(r < 0\) everywhere is no real change. Multiplying \(\eqref{eq:sl}\) by \(-1\) gives a problem with \(-r > 0\), \(-q\), the same \(p\), and eigenvalue \(-\lambda\). So we may as well assume \(r > 0\).
  • \(r = 0\) somewhere: there the coefficient of \(y''\) vanishes and the equation stops being a proper second-order equation. At an interior point this breaks the theory. At an endpoint it is allowed, and gives a singular problem (Section 4 below).
  • \(r\) changes sign: \(\mathcal{L}\) is still self-adjoint (Section VI never used the sign of \(r\)), but the eigenvalues lose their order. For \(r > 0\), integrating by parts gives \(\langle -(r u')', u angle = \int_a^b r\,|u'|^2\,dt\) up to boundary terms, which is nonnegative. This is what bounds the eigenvalues from below and makes them increase to \(+\infty\). If \(r\) changes sign, this quadratic form is indefinite, and eigenvalues can run off to both \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\).

2. From any second-order linear ODE to Sturm–Liouville form

Consider a general second-order linear equation with \(a(t) eq 0\) on \([a, b]\):

\[ a(t)\,x''(t) + b(t)\,x'(t) + c(t)\,x(t) = 0 . \]

Divide by \(a(t)\) and multiply by an integrating factor \(\mu(t)\) to be chosen:

\[ \mu\,x'' + \mu\, rac{b}{a}\,x' + \mu\, rac{c}{a}\,x = 0 . \]

We want the first two terms to be a single derivative, \((\mu\,x')' = \mu\,x'' + \mu'\,x'\). That requires \(\mu' = \mu\,b/a\), so

\[ \mu(t) = \exp\!\left(\int rac{b(t)}{a(t)}\,dt ight), \qquad ext{and then}\qquad ig(\mu\,x' ig)' + \mu\, rac{c}{a}\,x = 0 . \]

This is Sturm–Liouville form with \(r = \mu > 0\) and \(q = \mu c/a\). (For an eigenvalue problem \(a x'' + b x' + (c + \lambda d)\,x = 0\), the weight is \(p = \mu d/a\).) Every second-order linear ODE can be put in Sturm–Liouville form by multiplying by an integrating factor.

3. Eigenvalues are simple

In a regular Sturm–Liouville problem, each eigenvalue has only one eigenfunction, up to a constant factor. Suppose \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are eigenfunctions for the same \(\lambda\). Both satisfy the condition at \(t = a\), so, by the determinant argument of Section VI, their Wronskian vanishes there:

\[ W(a) = \det egin{bmatrix} y_1(a) & y_1'(a) \ y_2(a) & y_2'(a) \end{bmatrix} = 0 . \]

For two solutions of \(\eqref{eq:sl}\), \(r(t)\,W(t)\) is constant (Abel's identity: differentiate \(r(y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2)\) and use the equation). Since \(r > 0\), \(W(a) = 0\) forces \(W \equiv 0\), so \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are linearly dependent.

With periodic boundary conditions this argument fails, and an eigenvalue can have two independent eigenfunctions. For example, \(y'' + \lambda y = 0\) on \([-\pi, \pi]\) with \(y(-\pi) = y(\pi)\), \(y'(-\pi) = y'(\pi)\) has both \(\cos nt\) and \(\sin nt\) for \(\lambda = n^2\).

4. Regular, periodic and singular problems

  • Regular: a finite interval \([a, b]\), \(r > 0\) and \(p > 0\) on the whole closed interval, and separated boundary conditions \(\eqref{eq:bc}\).
  • Periodic: \(r(a) = r(b)\), with the conditions \(y(a) = y(b)\) and \(y'(a) = y'(b)\). The boundary term \(\eqref{eq:boundary}\) still cancels, so \(\mathcal{L}\) is self-adjoint, but eigenvalues may be double (as above). Ordinary Fourier series come from this case.
  • Singular: \(r\) vanishes at an endpoint (or the interval is infinite). At such an endpoint the usual condition is replaced by requiring \(y\) to stay bounded:
    • \(r(a) = 0\), with a condition \(A_2 y(b) + B_2 y'(b) = 0\) at \(t = b\);
    • \(r(b) = 0\), with a condition \(A_1 y(a) + B_1 y'(a) = 0\) at \(t = a\);
    • \(r(a) = r(b) = 0\), with no condition at either end (only boundedness).
    The boundary term vanishes because \(r = 0\) there, so \(\mathcal{L}\) is still self-adjoint.

For the classical singular problems, such as Legendre's equation on \([-1, 1]\) and Bessel's equation on \([0, R]\), the eigenfunctions are still complete. In general, though, a singular problem can also have a continuous spectrum. For example, on the whole real line the sum over eigenfunctions becomes an integral, and Fourier series become the Fourier transform [1].

5. What the theory is for

  • Sturm–Liouville theory does not give a faster way to solve a particular ODE, and it is not needed to show that solutions exist; ordinary ODE theory does that. What it guarantees is the structure of the solutions: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenfunctions, and completeness.
  • Completeness is the key for PDEs. It means any initial or boundary data \(f\) can be expanded as a generalized Fourier series, \(f = \sum_n c_n y_n\), and orthogonality gives each coefficient directly: \[ c_n = rac{\langle y_n, f angle_p}{\langle y_n, y_n angle_p} . \]
  • The functions are not arbitrary. \(r\) comes from the integrating factor (Section 2), and \(p\) comes from the physics of the problem; it often represents a non-uniform density or heat capacity. So the weighted inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot angle_p\), rather than the plain one, is forced on us by the problem.

IX. Examples from PDEs

1. The heat equation

Heat conduction in a rod with non-uniform material is described by

\[ rac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[r(x)\, rac{\partial u}{\partial x} ight] = ho(x)\, rac{\partial u}{\partial t}, \]

where \(u(x, t)\) is the temperature, \(r(x) > 0\) is the thermal conductivity, and \( ho(x) > 0\) is the heat capacity per unit length. Separate variables, \(u(x, t) = y(x)\,T(t)\):

\[ T(t)\, rac{d}{dx}\left[r(x)\, rac{dy}{dx} ight] = ho(x)\,y(x)\, rac{dT}{dt} . \]

Dividing by \( ho\,y\,T\), the left side depends only on \(x\) and the right side only on \(t\), so both equal a constant, which we call \(-\lambda\):

\[ rac{1}{ ho(x)\,y(x)}\, rac{d}{dx}\left[r(x)\, rac{dy}{dx} ight] = rac{1}{T(t)}\, rac{dT}{dt} = -\lambda . \]
  • Time equation: \(T'(t) = -\lambda\,T(t)\), so \(T(t) = C\,e^{-\lambda t}\).
  • Space equation, in Sturm–Liouville form with \(q = 0\) and weight \(p = ho\): \[ rac{d}{dx}\left[r(x)\, rac{dy}{dx} ight] + \lambda\, ho(x)\,y(x) = 0 . \]

With separated boundary conditions at the ends of the rod, the eigenfunctions \(y_n\) are orthogonal with weight \( ho\) and complete. So the solution for an initial temperature \(f(x)\) is

\[ u(x, t) = \sum_{n} c_n\,y_n(x)\,e^{-\lambda_n t}, \qquad c_n = rac{\langle y_n, f angle_ ho}{\langle y_n, y_n angle_ ho} . \]

2. The Schrödinger equation

\[ i\hbar\, rac{\partial \psi(x, t)}{\partial t} = - rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\, rac{\partial^2 \psi(x, t)}{\partial x^2} + V(x)\,\psi(x, t) . \]

Separate variables, \(\psi(x, t) = \psi(x)\,T(t)\), and divide by \(\psi(x)\,T(t)\):

\[ rac{i\hbar}{T(t)}\, rac{dT}{dt} = rac{1}{\psi(x)}\left(- rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\, rac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + V(x)\,\psi(x) ight) = E, \]

where the constant \(E\) is the energy.

  • Time equation: \(T'(t) = -\dfrac{iE}{\hbar}\,T(t)\), so \(T(t) = C\,e^{-iEt/\hbar}\).
  • Space equation, the time-independent Schrödinger equation: \[ - rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\, rac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + V(x)\,\psi = E\,\psi \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad rac{d}{dx}\left[ rac{\hbar^2}{2m}\, rac{d\psi}{dx} ight] + ig(-V(x) + E ig)\,\psi = 0 . \]

This is Sturm–Liouville form with \(r = \hbar^2/2m > 0\), \(q = -V\), \(p = 1\) and eigenvalue \(\lambda = E\). The operator \(\mathcal{L} = - rac{d}{dx} ig(r\, rac{d}{dx} ig) - q = - rac{\hbar^2}{2m} rac{d^2}{dx^2} + V\) is exactly the Hamiltonian. So Section VII explains two basic facts of quantum mechanics: energies are real, and states with different energies are orthogonal.

References

[1] William E. Boyce, Richard C. DiPrima and Douglas B. Meade. Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems, 11th edition. Wiley, 2017. Chapter 11.

[2] Wikipedia. “Sturm–Liouville theory.”

entry.title: The Continuity Equation
entry.content:
This post was revised with the help of ChatGPT.

This post walks through the continuity equation [1], from physical intuition to the mathematical statement. We derive it step by step and explain every quantity involved.

1. Motivation: conservation in physical systems

Many physical quantities are conserved, for example:

  • mass in a closed system;
  • charge in electromagnetism;
  • energy in an isolated system;
  • the number of particles in a fluid.

Although these quantities are conserved globally, they vary locally in space and time. To describe their local behavior, we use density functions. A density tells us how much of the conserved quantity there is per unit volume at each point and time:

  • mass density \( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)\);
  • charge density \( ho_q( oldsymbol{x}, t)\);
  • energy density \(\epsilon( oldsymbol{x}, t)\);
  • particle number density \(n( oldsymbol{x}, t)\).

Each of these is a function \(\mathbb{R}^n imes \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} o \mathbb{R}\).

To model how a density evolves, imagine the quantity being carried by a flow. A tiny fluid parcel at position \( oldsymbol{x}\) and time \(t\) moves with velocity \( oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t)\) and carries the local amount of the quantity with it.

Our goal is a local law describing how the density changes over space and time. This law is the continuity equation.

2. Basic definitions

Let:

  • \( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t): \mathbb{R}^n imes \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} o \mathbb{R}\) be the scalar density of a conserved quantity;
  • \( oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t): \mathbb{R}^n imes \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0} o \mathbb{R}^n\) be the flux. Its component along a unit vector \( oldsymbol{n}\) is the amount of the quantity crossing a unit area perpendicular to \( oldsymbol{n}\) per unit time.

When the quantity is transported by a velocity field \( oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t)\), the flux is

\[ oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) = ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t) .\]

In words, flux is density times velocity: how much passes through depends on how much is there and how fast it moves.

Now fix a region \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) with a smooth boundary \(\partial V\).

  • The total amount inside \(V\) at time \(t\) is

    \[Q_V(t) = \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

  • Its rate of change is

    \[ rac{d}{dt} Q_V(t) = rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

    Since the quantity is conserved (there are no sources or sinks), this change can only come from flux across the boundary \(\partial V\).

3. Flux across the boundary

Each point \( oldsymbol{x} \in \partial V\) has an outward unit normal \( oldsymbol{n}( oldsymbol{x})\). Let \(dS\) be the surface area element, and let \(d oldsymbol{S} = oldsymbol{n} \, dS\) be the oriented surface element, pointing outward.

The net outflow through \(\partial V\) per unit time is

\[\oint_{\partial V} oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \cdot d oldsymbol{S} .\]

The dot product keeps only the component of the flux normal to the surface; flow tangent to the surface does not cross it. The integral is positive when more of the quantity leaves than enters.

Conservation says that the amount inside decreases exactly at the rate it flows out:

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = - \oint_{\partial V} oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \cdot d oldsymbol{S} .\]

This is the integral form of the conservation law.

4. Gauss’s divergence theorem

To turn the boundary integral into a volume integral, we use the divergence theorem [2]. It holds for a continuously differentiable field \( oldsymbol{J}\):

\[\oint_{\partial V} oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \cdot d oldsymbol{S} = \int_V abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

The theorem says that the total outward flux through the boundary equals the total divergence inside:

  • the left-hand side adds up what flows out of each patch of the surface;
  • the right-hand side adds up the local “spreading out” of the flow at each point inside \(V\).

Substituting into the conservation law gives

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = - \int_V abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

5. From integral form to differential form

If \( ho\) is smooth enough (see Section 8), we may move the time derivative inside the integral:

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = \int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

Thus

\[\int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} = - \int_V abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} ,\]

and moving everything to one side,

\[\int_V \left( rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} + abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) ight) d oldsymbol{x} = 0 .\]

This holds for every region \(V\). If the integrand \(g = \partial_t ho + abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}\) is continuous, it must vanish pointwise. To see why, suppose \(g( oldsymbol{x}_0, t) > 0\) at some point. By continuity, \(g > 0\) on a small ball \(B\) around \( oldsymbol{x}_0\), and then \(\int_B g \, d oldsymbol{x} > 0\), a contradiction. The same argument works if \(g( oldsymbol{x}_0, t) < 0\). Therefore

\[ rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} + abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) = 0 .\]

6. The continuity equation

Using \( oldsymbol{J} = ho \, oldsymbol{v}\), we obtain the continuity equation:

\[ egin{equation} rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} + abla \cdot ig( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, oldsymbol{v}( oldsymbol{x}, t) ig) = 0 . \label{eq:continuity} \end{equation}\]

It expresses the local conservation of the quantity carried by the flow.

Expanded form. By the product rule, \( abla \cdot ( ho oldsymbol{v}) = oldsymbol{v} \cdot abla ho + ho \, abla \cdot oldsymbol{v}\), so

\[\underbrace{ rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} + oldsymbol{v} \cdot abla ho}_{\displaystyle rac{D ho}{Dt}} = - ho \, abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} .\]

The left-hand side is the material derivative \(D ho / Dt\), the rate of change of density seen by an observer moving with a parcel. So the density following a parcel changes only when the flow compresses (\( abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} < 0\)) or expands (\( abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} > 0\)). For an incompressible flow (\( abla \cdot oldsymbol{v} = 0\)), the density along each parcel stays constant.

7. Divergence: geometric meaning

The divergence of a vector field is

\[ abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}, t) = \sum_{i=1}^n rac{\partial J_i( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial x_i} .\]

By the continuity equation, \(\partial_t ho = - abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}\). So:

  • if \( abla \cdot oldsymbol{J} > 0\) at a point, more flows out than in, and \( ho\) decreases there;
  • if \( abla \cdot oldsymbol{J} < 0\), more flows in than out, and \( ho\) increases;
  • if \( abla \cdot oldsymbol{J} = 0\), inflow and outflow balance, and \( ho\) does not change there.

Geometrically, divergence is a local measure of how much a vector field “spreads out” at a point. This follows from the divergence theorem: shrink \(V\) to a small ball \(B_r( oldsymbol{x})\) around a point, and

\[ abla \cdot oldsymbol{J}( oldsymbol{x}) = \lim_{r o 0} rac{1}{\lvert B_r vert} \oint_{\partial B_r} oldsymbol{J} \cdot d oldsymbol{S} ,\]

i.e. divergence is the outward flux per unit volume.

8. Why can we swap the derivative and the integral?

We used

\[ rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} = \int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} .\]

By definition of the derivative,

\[ egin{align*} rac{d}{dt} \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} &= \lim_{\Delta t o 0} rac{1}{\Delta t} \left( \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + \Delta t) \, d oldsymbol{x} - \int_V ho( oldsymbol{x}, t) \, d oldsymbol{x} ight) \[1ex] &= \lim_{\Delta t o 0} \int_V rac{ ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + \Delta t) - ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\Delta t} \, d oldsymbol{x} \[1ex] &\overset{(\star)}{=} \int_V \lim_{\Delta t o 0} rac{ ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + \Delta t) - ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\Delta t} \, d oldsymbol{x} = \int_V rac{\partial ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)}{\partial t} \, d oldsymbol{x} . \end{align*}\]

The step \((\star)\), which swaps the limit and the integral, is the only one that needs justification. A sufficient condition is that \(V\) is bounded and \(\partial_t ho\) is continuous on \(\overline{V} imes [t - \delta, t + \delta]\). By the mean value theorem, the difference quotient equals \(\partial_t ho( oldsymbol{x}, t + heta \Delta t)\) for some \( heta \in (0, 1)\). This is uniformly bounded, so the dominated convergence theorem applies. (The region \(V\) is fixed in time. For a region that moves with the flow, you would need the Reynolds transport theorem instead.)

9. Summary

We began with:

  • a physical idea: a conserved quantity;
  • a model: the quantity is carried by a flow with velocity \( oldsymbol{v}\);
  • a density \( ho( oldsymbol{x}, t)\) and a flux \( oldsymbol{J} = ho oldsymbol{v}\);
  • a balance law: rate of change inside a region = \(-\)(net outflow through its boundary);
  • the divergence theorem: surface integral \( o\) volume integral;
  • swapping derivative and integral: \( rac{d}{dt}\int_V = \int_V \partial_t\);
  • “zero integral over every region” \(\Rightarrow\) “zero integrand.”

We arrived at

\[ rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} + abla \cdot ( ho \, oldsymbol{v}) = 0 .\]

The continuity equation appears whenever we model a conserved quantity moving through space. It captures one simple idea:

Any local change in the quantity must be explained by its flow into or out of that region.

It is fundamental across physics and mathematics: in fluid mechanics, electromagnetism (conservation of charge), quantum mechanics (conservation of probability), and, more recently, in the flow-matching and diffusion models of machine learning, where it describes how a probability density is transported by a learned velocity field.

References

[1] Wikipedia. “Continuity equation.”

[2] Wikipedia. “Divergence theorem.”
entry.summary: Deriving the continuity equation step by step, from conservation laws to the divergence theorem.

entry.title: LC-3 Brief Review
entry.content:
This is a brief review of some topics from ECE 220. All code below is LC-3 assembly; the code blocks use NASM syntax highlighting, which is close enough.

I. Purpose and description

1. Purpose

This program reviews:

  1. LC-3 basics, including I/O;
  2. the run-time stack;
  3. recursion in LC-3;
  4. linked lists in LC-3;
  5. binary trees in LC-3.

2. Description

  1. The program is a direct LC-3 translation of a C program that prints a directory structure.
  2. The directory tree is stored in memory in fixed data structures. The program prints it to the console in a pre-order traversal, in the format shown in Desired output.
  3. To show how C is translated into assembly, every user-defined C function uses the run-time stack. I also wrote my own versions of the OUT and PUTS system calls, which C’s printf() would ultimately rely on. They are called PRINT_A_CHAR and PRINT_A_STRING. Like real system calls, they do not use the run-time stack. They work the same way as the OUT and PUTS trap service routines in the LC-3 operating system.
  4. The test case is not exhaustive. Gemini generated most of it, and I fixed a few syntax errors so that it assembles. Feel free to add more test cases.

3. Data structure design

(1) Files and folders

A file node (a node of a singly linked list):

  • [0] next pointer: the next file in the same folder (NULL if none);
  • [1] pointer to the file name (.STRINGZ).

A folder node (a node of a binary tree):

  • [0] left pointer: the left child (NULL if none);
  • [1] right pointer: the right child (NULL if none);
  • [2] file pointer: the head of this folder’s file list (NULL if none);
  • [3] pointer to the folder name (.STRINGZ).

Both children of a folder are sub-folders of it. The tree is a plain binary tree, not a “left-child, right-sibling” encoding.

(2) Folder tree (test case)

                         root
                /                   \
          projects                  media
          /      \               /         \
    c_project    blog      documents       photos
     /     \                /      \           \
 utils  python_project  reports  presentations  travel
                                                    \
                                                 sub_travel

(3) Files in each folder (test case)

  • root: config.sys
  • projects: README.md
  • c_project: main.c → Makefile
  • utils: helper.c
  • python_project: main.py → requirements.txt
  • blog: index.md
  • media: (empty)
  • documents: meeting_notes.docx → todo_list.txt
  • reports: q1_report.pdf → budget_summary.xlsx
  • presentations: project_kickoff.pptx
  • photos: IMG001.jpg → IMG002.jpg
  • travel: trip.txt → map.png
  • sub_travel: packing_list.md

(4) C structs and function prototypes

4. Desired output

root
    file: config.sys
    projects
        file: README.md
        c_project
            file: main.c Makefile
            utils
                file: helper.c
            python_project
                file: main.py requirements.txt
        blog
            file: index.md
    media
        documents
            file: meeting_notes.docx todo_list.txt
            reports
                file: q1_report.pdf budget_summary.xlsx
            presentations
                file: project_kickoff.pptx
        photos
            file: IMG001.jpg IMG002.jpg
            travel
                file: trip.txt map.png
                sub_travel
                    file: packing_list.md

5. Conventions

These conventions follow the run-time stack model from our textbook [1], as best I remember it. Please let me know if you spot a mistake.

Registers:

  • R4: global data pointer (not needed in this program)
  • R5: frame pointer (points to the first local variable)
  • R6: stack pointer (points to the top element of the stack)
  • R7: return address (written by JSR and TRAP)

The stack frame of one function call (the stack grows toward lower addresses):

Address Contents
M[R5 - k] further local variables (if any)
M[R5 + 0] first local variable
M[R5 + 1] caller’s frame pointer
M[R5 + 2] return address
M[R5 + 3] return value (reserved even for void functions)
M[R5 + 4] first argument
M[R5 + 5] second argument, …

Other conventions:

  1. Arguments and local variables are accessed through R5 plus an offset, never through R6, because R6 moves whenever something is pushed.
  2. The caller pushes arguments from right to left, so the first argument ends up nearest the frame. On return, the callee leaves R6 pointing at the return value, and the caller pops the return value and the arguments.

Notes on this program:

  1. Each of print_folder(), print_file(), and print_space() has exactly one local variable (current, next, and i), stored at M[R5 + 0].
  2. main() does not build a frame and leaves R5 unset. This is fine here, because main never reads R5, and every callee saves and restores R5 itself.

II. LC-3 translation of the C functions

3. print_file()

Saving R0 in a fixed memory location like PRINT_FILE_SAVE_R0 only works because print_file() is not recursive. A recursive function would overwrite the saved value on each nested call, so it would have to save registers on the stack instead.

4. print_space()

III. PRINT_A_CHAR and PRINT_A_STRING “system calls”

entry.title: The Gaussian Integral
entry.content:
This post introduces the Gaussian integral, starting from basic integration and building up to a probabilistic and linear-algebraic view of it.

I. The fundamental integral

The most basic Gaussian integral is

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2}x^2 \right) dx = \sqrt{2\pi} ,\]

or equivalently, in the form of the standard Gaussian density,

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} x^2 \right) dx = 1 .\]

Here is how to compute it. Write \(I\) for the integral.

Step 1: square it

\[\begin{align*} I^2 &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} x^2 \right) dx \cdot \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} y^2 \right) dy \\[1ex] &= \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2}(x^2 + y^2) \right) dx \, dy . \end{align*}\]

The integrand is positive, so Tonelli’s theorem allows us to combine the two integrals into a double integral.

Step 2: switch to polar coordinates

Let

\[\left\{ \begin{aligned} x &= r \cos \theta \\ y &= r \sin \theta \end{aligned} \right. \qquad r \in [0, \infty), \ \theta \in [0, 2\pi) .\]

The Jacobian matrix of this map is

\[J(r, \theta) = \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (r, \theta)} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial r} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial \theta} \\[1.5ex] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial r} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & - r \sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & r \cos \theta \end{bmatrix} ,\]

so the area element transforms as

\[\begin{align*} dx \, dy &= \left\lvert \det J(r, \theta) \right\rvert \, dr \, d\theta \\[1ex] &= r \left( \cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta \right) dr \, d\theta \\[1ex] &= r \, dr \, d\theta . \end{align*}\]

Step 3: integrate

\[\begin{align*} I^2 &= \int_0^{2 \pi} \int_0^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} r^2 \right) r \, dr \, d\theta \\[1ex] &= \int_0^{2 \pi} \left[ -\exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} r^2 \right) \right]_0^{\infty} d\theta \\[1ex] &= \int_0^{2 \pi} 1 \, d\theta = 2 \pi . \end{align*}\]

Since \(I > 0\),

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} x^2 \right) dx = \sqrt{2 \pi} .\]

Shifting and scaling. Substituting \(x \mapsto (x - b)/\sqrt{a}\) gives, for any \(a > 0\) and \(b \in \mathbb{R}\),

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - b)^2}{2a} \right) dx = \sqrt{2 \pi a} ,\]

or, in the form of a Gaussian density,

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi a}} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - b)^2}{2 a} \right) dx = 1 .\]

II. From one dimension to many

Now we generalize the univariate Gaussian integral to \(n\) dimensions.

Notation.

  1. \(\boldsymbol{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is a column vector.
  2. \(d\boldsymbol{x}\) denotes the volume element \(dx_1 \cdots dx_n\).
  3. For \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(\boldsymbol{x}) \, d \boldsymbol{x} = \idotsint_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x_1, \dots, x_n) \, dx_1 \cdots dx_n\).

Statement. Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) be symmetric positive definite, and let \(\boldsymbol{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n\). Then

\[\begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top A^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d\boldsymbol{x} = \sqrt{ (2 \pi)^n \det A } . \label{eq:multivariate} \end{equation}\]

For \(n = 1\) and \(A = a\), this is exactly the shifted and scaled formula above.

Step 1: diagonalize

Since \(A\) is symmetric positive definite, so is \(A^{-1}\). By the spectral theorem [1],

\[A^{-1} = Q^\top \Lambda Q ,\]

where \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\) has positive diagonal entries and \(Q\) is orthogonal (\(Q^\top Q = Q Q^\top = I\)).

Change variables to

\[\boldsymbol{y} = Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) , \qquad \text{i.e.} \quad y_i = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} Q_{ij} (x_j - b_j) .\]

Then \(\partial y_i / \partial x_k = Q_{ik}\), so the Jacobian matrix is \(\partial \boldsymbol{y} / \partial \boldsymbol{x} = Q\). An orthogonal matrix satisfies \(\det(Q)^2 = \det(Q^\top Q) = 1\), so \(\det Q = \pm 1\). (It can be \(-1\), for a reflection. That is why the absolute value matters.) Hence

\[d \boldsymbol{y} = \left\lvert \det Q \right\rvert d \boldsymbol{x} = d \boldsymbol{x} .\]

Substituting,

\[\begin{align*} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top A^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d\boldsymbol{x} \\[1ex] ={} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top Q^\top \Lambda Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d \boldsymbol{x} \\[1ex] ={} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \big(Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \big)^\top \Lambda \big(Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \big) \right) d \boldsymbol{x} \\[1ex] ={} &\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} \right) d \boldsymbol{y} . \end{align*}\]

Step 2: separate the variables

Because \(\Lambda\) is diagonal,

\[\boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 & \cdots & y_n \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & \lambda_n \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{bmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i y_i^2 ,\]

so the exponential factors into a product, and so does the integral:

\[\begin{align*} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} \right) d \boldsymbol{y} &= \idotsint_{\mathbb{R}^n} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \lambda_i y_i^2 \right) dy_1 \cdots dy_n \\[1ex] &= \prod_{i=1}^{n} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} \lambda_i y_i^2 \right) dy_i . \end{align*}\]

Step 3: use the one-dimensional result

Each factor is a one-dimensional Gaussian integral with \(a = 1/\lambda_i\):

\[\prod_{i=1}^{n} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp \left( -\frac{y_i^2}{2 \lambda_i^{-1}} \right) dy_i = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \sqrt{\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda_i}} = \frac{(2 \pi)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det \Lambda}} .\]

Finally, from \(A^{-1} = Q^\top \Lambda Q\),

\[\frac{1}{\det A} = \det (A^{-1}) = \det(Q^\top) \det(\Lambda) \det(Q) = \det(Q)^2 \det \Lambda = \det \Lambda .\]

Putting everything together,

\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b})^\top A^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{b}) \right) d\boldsymbol{x} = \frac{(2 \pi)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{\det \Lambda}} = \sqrt{ (2 \pi)^n \det A } ,\]

which proves \(\eqref{eq:multivariate}\). \(\blacksquare\)

III. Probability and linear algebra

1. The univariate Gaussian distribution

If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), its density integrates to one:

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x) \, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2} \right) dx = 1 .\]

This is just the shifted and scaled formula from Part I: the mean \(\mu\) plays the role of the shift \(b\), and the variance \(\sigma^2\) plays the role of the scale \(a\).

2. The multivariate Gaussian distribution

We write a random vector in bold capitals, \(\boldsymbol{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_n)^\top\). Each component \(X_i\) is a random variable. A specific value of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is written in bold lowercase, \(\boldsymbol{x}\).

If \(\boldsymbol{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)\) with a positive definite covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), then by \(\eqref{eq:multivariate}\) with \(A = \Sigma\) and \(\boldsymbol{b} = \boldsymbol{\mu}\),

\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}) \, d \boldsymbol{x} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^n \det \Sigma}} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{2} (\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right) d \boldsymbol{x} = 1 .\]

The interesting part is the change of variables that simplified the quadratic form in the exponent. It has a clear probabilistic meaning.

(1) Diagonalizing \(\Sigma^{-1}\): the PCA view

Write

\[\Sigma^{-1} = Q^\top \Lambda Q ,\]

where the rows of the orthogonal matrix \(Q\) are eigenvectors of \(\Sigma^{-1}\), and \(\Lambda\) holds the corresponding eigenvalues. The eigenvectors of \(\Sigma^{-1}\) are the same as those of \(\Sigma\), but each eigenvalue is inverted: \(\Sigma = Q^\top \Lambda^{-1} Q\).

This is exactly the core idea of principal component analysis (PCA) [2]. We find the principal axes of the distribution and rotate the coordinate system to align with them. The variance along the \(i\)-th axis is \(1/\lambda_i\), so the direction of largest variance belongs to the smallest eigenvalue of \(\Sigma^{-1}\).

(2) The change of variables

Apply

\[\boldsymbol{y} = Q (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) , \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad \boldsymbol{Y} = Q (\boldsymbol{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) .\]

This centers and rotates the coordinate system, and the quadratic form becomes

\[(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) = \boldsymbol{y}^\top \Lambda \boldsymbol{y} .\]

The covariance of the new random vector is

\[\mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{Y}) = \mathbb{E}\left[\boldsymbol{Y} \boldsymbol{Y}^\top\right] = Q \, \Sigma \, Q^\top = Q \left( Q^\top \Lambda^{-1} Q \right) Q^\top = \Lambda^{-1} ,\]

which is diagonal. So the components \(Y_1, \dots, Y_n\) are uncorrelated, with \(\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = 1/\lambda_i\). Going from \(\boldsymbol{X}\) to \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) decorrelates the coordinates.

(3) Uncorrelated vs. independent

In general, uncorrelated random variables need not be independent. But for a jointly Gaussian random vector, uncorrelated components are independent. (Marginally Gaussian is not enough: the vector must be jointly Gaussian.) Here \(\boldsymbol{Y}\) is an affine function of a Gaussian vector, so it is jointly Gaussian.

You can see this directly from the density, which factors into a product of one-dimensional Gaussians:

\[f_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{y}) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\lambda_i^{-1}}} \exp\left( -\frac{y_i^2}{2\lambda_i^{-1}} \right) = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathcal{N}\!\left(y_i;\, 0,\, \lambda_i^{-1}\right) .\]

This factorization is exactly what made the integral in Part II easy to compute.

Thanks to ChatGPT, which helped me organize my words.

References

[1] David Vogan. “Proof of the spectral theorem.” Lecture notes, MIT, 2013.

[2] Jonathon Shlens. “A Tutorial on Principal Component Analysis.” 2005.
